Are all bodies with decisive authority o.note: In a locally hosted scenario the enterprise itself is the operator and controller. Assuming an EU-headquartered company, all decisive authority rests with in-house IT management under EU jurisdiction. No external provider entity exists that could be subject to non-EU law or acquisition.

Does the provider have structural or con.note: There is no external cloud provider that could be acquired or subject to change of control. The enterprise owns and controls its infrastructure outright. The self-hosted model structurally eliminates the acquisition-risk vector that affects all third-party cloud providers.

Does the provider rely primarily on fina.note: Infrastructure CapEx is financed from the EU organisation's own internal budget. However hardware procurement flows to non-EU vendors (Dell, HP, Intel, AMD), meaning a material share of investment leaves EU jurisdiction. No external investor dependency, but no EU-institution financing either.

Does the provider demonstrate significan.note: EU-based IT staff are employed to operate the infrastructure, generating internal EU employment and value. However this is a company cost centre rather than a cloud provider creating value for third parties. Investment scale is limited to the organisation's own operational needs with no broader EU economic multiplier.

Is the provider actively involved in EU.note: Individual enterprises running on-premise infrastructure are not GAIA-X members or participants in formal EU digital sovereignty initiatives. BSI C5 and ENISA EUCS are cloud-provider frameworks. Self-hosted deployments align with sovereignty goals by design but do not participate in EU-level cloud governance programmes.

Can the provider sustain secure operatio.note: No cloud provider can be suspended by non-EU authority. However critical software licenses (Windows Server, VMware/Broadcom, Oracle) and hardware support contracts are with non-EU vendors. If those vendors withdrew support under legal compulsion, continued operations would require migration to open-source alternatives — feasible with planning but not immediate.

Is the provider governed exclusively by.note: The 'provider' is the EU-based enterprise itself, incorporated under its member state's legal system. No third-party cloud provider is involved. All data processing, employment law, and operational governance are subject exclusively to EU and national law.

Is the provider free from non-EU laws wi.note: A locally hosted deployment with no US cloud provider and no US-headquartered services in the data path is free from US CLOUD Act jurisdiction. No Chinese Cybersecurity Law exposure. Data does not transit or reside on any non-EU third-party infrastructure.

Are there no legal, contractual, or tech.note: No third-party cloud provider with a non-EU parent exists to receive compelled access orders. Data is physically held on-premise under direct enterprise control. Lawful access is only possible via EU judicial or regulatory authority targeting the enterprise directly, governed by EU law.

Is the provider free from international.note: Data remains entirely on-premise within EU jurisdiction. No cross-border transfer to non-EU countries. US EAR or ITAR export control regimes do not apply to data processing on EU-internal infrastructure without US-origin controlled technology explicitly in the processing path.

Is the provider's intellectual property.note: The enterprise's own application and configuration IP is EU-owned and developed. However the underlying infrastructure IP — server firmware (Intel, AMD), hypervisor (VMware/Broadcom), and OS (Microsoft Windows Server) — is typically non-EU. A fully open-source stack (Linux, KVM) reduces but does not eliminate this exposure.

Does the customer retain exclusive crypt.note: In a self-hosted environment, the enterprise generates, stores, and rotates all encryption keys internally with no third-party involvement. On-premise HSMs (Hardware Security Modules) can be deployed for FIPS 140-2/3 compliant key management. Full cryptographic sovereignty is a direct benefit of local hosting.

Does the provider offer full auditabilit.note: Full auditability is technically achievable on-premise (SIEM, syslog, access logging) but requires deliberate implementation. Unlike managed cloud services with built-in audit trails, on-premise environments depend entirely on the organisation's own tooling maturity. Audit gaps are common without a dedicated logging programme.

Does the provider guarantee irreversible.note: Data deletion is fully under enterprise control but verifiable evidence of irreversible removal requires deliberate processes: cryptographic erasure, DoD 5220.22-M or Blancco-certified wiping, and destruction certificates for physical media. These must be actively implemented rather than being provided automatically.

Is all data storage and processing stric.note: All data physically resides on-premise at EU office locations. No third-country fallback, replication to non-EU infrastructure, or cloud-side backup. Data location sovereignty is absolute in a properly configured local deployment, subject only to the organisation's own backup and DR strategy.

Are AI models and data pipelines develop.note: If AI is deployed locally (e.g. Ollama, vLLM with open-weight models on-premise GPU servers) governance is entirely EU-controlled. However most enterprises also use SaaS AI tools (Microsoft Copilot, OpenAI API, Google Vertex) that route data to non-EU infrastructure, creating mixed AI sovereignty. Verdict assumes a typical enterprise scenario without fully local AI.

Can workloads be migrated to alternative.note: Portability depends on the technology stack in use. Virtualised workloads on open hypervisors (KVM, Proxmox) using standard disk images are highly portable to EU cloud providers. Workloads on proprietary platforms (VMware vSphere, Windows Server, proprietary databases) face meaningful lock-in. Migration is feasible but requires architectural planning.

Can EU operators fully manage and mainta.note: Day-to-day operations are managed by EU-based internal IT staff. However hardware support contracts (Dell ProSupport, HP Care Pack, Lenovo support — all non-EU vendors) and proprietary software maintenance (Microsoft, VMware) require vendor involvement for patches, firmware, and hardware replacement.

Does an EU-based talent pool exist to op.note: The organisation's own EU-based IT team operates the infrastructure. The EU has a broad talent pool of infrastructure engineers, system administrators, and DevOps professionals capable of running on-premise deployments. No dependency on non-EU operational talent for standard IT operations.

Is all operational support delivered exc.note: Internal IT support is entirely EU-based. However hardware vendor support desks (Dell, HP, Lenovo) and software vendor support (Microsoft, VMware) may route tickets to non-EU support centres. Remote-access support sessions from non-EU vendor engineers represent a potential data exposure channel that must be contractually managed.

Is full technical documentation and sour.note: If the stack is open-source (Linux, KVM, PostgreSQL, OpenStack), full source code and documentation are available under open licences guaranteeing long-term autonomy. Proprietary components (Windows Server, VMware, Oracle DB) provide documentation but no source code access, creating dependency on vendor continuity and pricing.

Are all critical suppliers and subcontra.note: Critical hardware suppliers (Dell US, HP Inc. US, Lenovo China, Supermicro US) and software suppliers (Microsoft US, VMware/Broadcom US, Intel US, AMD US) are predominantly non-EU. This is an inherent structural limitation of the current global technology supply chain affecting all on-premise deployments equally.

Is key hardware manufactured or assemble.note: Enterprise server hardware is dominated by non-EU manufacturers: Dell (US), HP (US), Lenovo (China), Supermicro (US). No major EU-origin server OEM exists for standard x86 infrastructure. Some EU assembly occurs (e.g. Dell in Limerick, Ireland) but core components and IP originate from non-EU countries. Is firmware and embedded code controllin.note: All x86 server firmware is non-EU: Intel Management Engine (US), AMD Platform Security Processor (US), UEFI/BIOS from AMI (US) or Insyde (Taiwan). No EU-origin firmware alternative exists for standard enterprise hardware. This constraint is universal across all providers and hosting models in this survey.

Is the software stack architected, packa.note: Open-source components (Linux kernel, KVM, PostgreSQL, Apache) are developed by global communities with significant EU contributors but are not exclusively EU-architected. Proprietary components (Windows Server, VMware) are US-architected and US-updated. A fully open-source stack improves EU software control but the OS and tools remain globally developed.

Is the provider free from significant re.note: On-premise infrastructure has significant structural dependency on non-EU vendors: Intel/AMD for processors, US or Chinese OEMs for servers, Microsoft/VMware for virtualisation and OS in typical enterprise deployments. Migrating to a fully EU-supply-chain stack is not currently achievable with standard commercial hardware.

Does the provider offer full transparenc.note: The organisation has direct visibility into its own procurement and configuration. However hardware vendor supply chains (chip fabs, component sourcing, firmware build processes) are opaque and not auditable by the enterprise. Independent security audits of on-premise infrastructure are fully possible and under the enterprise's direct control.

Does the provider use well-documented, n.note: Open standards are achievable on-premise (REST APIs, OpenAPI, S3-compatible storage via MinIO, OpenStack) but require deliberate architectural choices. Many enterprises run proprietary interfaces (Microsoft Active Directory, VMware vSphere APIs, Oracle) that reduce interoperability. The verdict depends on the specific technology decisions made internally.

Is the software stack available under op.note: A fully open-source on-premise stack (Linux, KVM, Ceph, PostgreSQL, OpenStack) is achievable and would yield a Y. However most enterprise environments combine open-source with proprietary software (Windows Server, VMware, Oracle, SAP), making this partial in practice. The organisation has full control over the composition of its stack.

Does the provider offer full architectur.note: As the infrastructure owner, the enterprise has complete architectural transparency. All data flows, network topology, and component dependencies are documented and auditable by the organisation itself. No hidden vendor-side processing or black-box services exist in a purely on-premise deployment.

Is the provider free from dependency on.note: All standard enterprise compute relies on Intel or AMD x86 processors (both US) and NVIDIA/AMD GPUs for ML/AI workloads (both US). No EU-origin processor is commercially available for enterprise server deployment. The EuroHPC Joint Undertaking is developing EU HPC chips but these are not yet available for standard enterprise on-premise use.

Does the provider hold recognised EU cer.note: Office-hosted environments are rarely ISO 27001 certified unless the organisation has invested in a formal ISMS programme. BSI C5 and ENISA EUCS are cloud service provider certifications and are not applicable to on-premise enterprise deployments. Certification is achievable but requires significant investment and is atypical for standard office infrastructure.

Is the provider fully compliant with GDP.note: GDPR obligations apply to any EU organisation processing personal data regardless of hosting model. NIS2 compliance depends on whether the organisation falls within a critical sector scope. DORA applies only to financial entities. Full compliance requires deliberate policy implementation — the on-premise model neither guarantees nor prevents compliance.

Are all Security Operations Centres oper.note: Larger EU enterprises may operate an internal SOC staffed exclusively by EU employees. However many organisations rely on managed SOC services from non-EU-headquartered providers (IBM Security, Palo Alto, CrowdStrike — all US). Without a dedicated in-house EU SOC, security monitoring may involve non-EU data processing.

Does the provider give customers direct.note: The organisation is both operator and customer, retaining full unrestricted access to all security monitoring, logging systems, and alerting. No intermediary can restrict log access. This complete self-oversight is a fundamental sovereignty advantage of on-premise over any third-party cloud model.

Does the provider follow EU-compliant br.note: GDPR Art. 33 72-hour breach notification applies to all EU data controllers regardless of hosting model. Patch management is fully independent — no vendor push without consent — but requires an internal patch governance process. Unpatched systems are a known on-premise risk without disciplined patch management procedures.

Can EU entities perform independent secu.note: Full physical and logical access to on-premise infrastructure enables comprehensive independent security audits without restriction. EU regulatory authorities (BSI, ANSSI, national supervisory bodies) can conduct on-site audits. Penetration testing, source code review, and architecture assessment can all be performed with complete access — no vendor permission required.

Does the provider operate energy-efficie.note: Office server rooms and on-premise data closets typically operate at PUE 1.5–2.5, significantly above the 1.1–1.4 range of modern hyperscale data centres. No published PUE targets exist for enterprise on-premise deployments. Cooling and power infrastructure designed for office use rather than IT workloads results in inherent energy inefficiency at this scale.

Does the provider apply circular economy.note: EU WEEE Directive requires electronic waste recycling for all organisations. Most EU enterprises comply with basic WEEE obligations for hardware disposal. However proactive circular economy practices (server refurbishment programmes, component reuse, extended lifecycle management) as seen in leading cloud providers are rarely implemented at enterprise scale.

Does the provider publish transparent ca.note: Enterprise on-premise IT carbon footprint is rarely broken out and published separately. EU CSRD requires large companies to report Scope 1/2/3 emissions from 2024–2026 at a group level, but IT infrastructure-specific disclosures at the granularity of cloud provider sustainability reports are not typical of enterprise on-premise environments.

Does the provider source renewable or lo.note: Renewable energy sourcing depends entirely on the organisation's energy procurement strategy and its national grid carbon intensity. EU member states vary significantly in renewable mix. Organisations can purchase renewable energy certificates (RECs/GOs) or sign Power Purchase Agreements independently of their hosting model — no inherent advantage or disadvantage versus cloud.

local-hosting.summary_note: Local (on-premise) hosting at an EU enterprise office represents the highest possible data-location sovereignty and legal jurisdiction clarity: no third-party cloud provider, no CLOUD Act exposure, no risk of a provider being acquired by a non-EU entity, and complete cryptographic key control. The enterprise retains full physical and logical control over its data and infrastructure. However this model scores poorly on supply chain and environmental dimensions — standard enterprise hardware (Dell, HP, Lenovo, Intel, AMD) is entirely non-EU in origin and firmware, and office server rooms operate far less efficiently than modern data centres (PUE 1.5–2.5 vs 1.1–1.4). Operational sovereignty is also partial: critical software dependencies (Windows Server, VMware, Oracle) and hardware support contracts remain with non-EU vendors, meaning true independence requires deliberate migration to an open-source stack. The on-premise model trades cloud-provider risk for vendor dependency risk and operational overhead. For EU enterprises prioritising data location control, absence of third-party access channels, and legal sovereignty, local hosting is the strongest option in this survey. For scalability, feature richness, energy efficiency, and cost predictability, it is the weakest.
